                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF

                DR. JAIME LYNDSEY MCGOVERN

                       ON BEHALF OF

                       WALMART INC.




                       November 30, 2026

                      Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                         Walmart Inc.


 1   Introduction.
 2   Q.    PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME, BUSINESS ADDRESS, AND OCCUPATION.

 3   A.   My name is Jaime L. McGovern, Ph.D. My business address is Always Building,

 4        814 Respect Dr., Bentonville, Arkansas 72716. I am employed by Walmart Inc.

 5        (“Walmart”) as Senior Manager, Utility Partnerships – Regulatory.

 6   Q.   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING IN THIS CASE?

 7   A.   I am testifying on behalf of Walmart.

 8   Q.   ARE YOU THE SAME DR. MCGOVERN WHO SUBMITTED DIRECT

 9        TESTIMONY IN THIS CASE ON BEHALF OF WALMART?

10   A.   Yes.

11

12   Purpose of Rebuttal Testimony
13   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

14   A.   The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to respond to the direct testimonies

15        submitted by certain other parties in this proceeding concerning cost allocation,

16        large-load tariffs, and related rate-design issues proposed in the amended application

17        filed by El Paso Electric Company (“EPE” or “Company”). Specifically, my

18        testimony addresses positions advanced by the Coalition for Clean Affordable

19        Energy (“CCAE”), New Mexico Public Regulation – Utility Division Staff (“Staff”),

20        the City of Las Cruces and Doña Ana County (“CLC/DAC”), and the U.S.

21        Department of Defense and other Federal Executive Agencies (“DOD/FEA”), and

22        the New Mexico Department of Justice (“NMDOJ”). Walmart continues to support




                                             1
                                 NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                      Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                         Walmart Inc.


 1        rates based on demonstrated cost causation, protection against unrecovered

2         customer-specific investment, and a specialized large-load framework for genuinely

3         distinct new or incremental load. Walmart does not support using a customer’s

4         industry, technology, ordinary commercial growth, or numerical size alone as a

5         substitute for a record-specific showing of different costs or risks.

6    Q.   PLEASE      PROVIDE A SUMMARY OF WALMART’S                              REBUTTAL

7         RECOMMENDATIONS.

8    A.   Walmart recommends that the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission

9         (“Commission”):

10        (1) permit consideration of transparent supplemental class cost-of-service

11        presentations, but use any alternative presentation to reset class revenue

12        responsibility only after a complete evidentiary review;

13        (2) require the inclusion of properly recoverable battery capacity costs in base rates

14        so that they are examined in the class cost-of-service study;

15        (3) require use an accurate and transparent class cost-of-service study as the

16        precursor to inform revenue allocation, and then preserve the existing revenue-

17        allocation position subject to the final authorized revenue requirement;

18        (4) require customer-specific recovery only for demonstrated incremental costs and

19        risks caused by qualifying new load;

20        (5) require preservation of the existing customers’ rate-schedule flexibility and

21        prohibit automatic migration to Rate Nos. 50 or 51; and




                                             2
                                      NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                           Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                              Walmart Inc.


 1            (6) permit the application of any specialized large-load framework only to new or

 2            incremental single-site load that satisfies objective, like-with-like criteria, including

 3            Walmart’s recommended 75-megawatt entrance threshold.

 4   Q.       DOES THIS REBUTTAL TESTIMONY CHANGE WALMART’S DIRECT

 5            TESTIMONY RECOMMENDATIONS?

 6   A.       No. Walmart continues to recommend that the Commission use the appropriate

 7            overall revenue requirement when considering revenue allocation and rate design;

 8            preserve the flexibility of existing customers; and apply any specialized large-load

 9            tariff only to genuinely new or incremental load at a single point of delivery that

10            satisfies objective, cost-causative eligibility criteria.

11

12   Class Cost of Service and Revenue Allocation
13   Q.    WHAT DOES STAFF PROPOSE REGARDING A PROBABILITY-OF-

14            DISPATCH OR OTHER HOURLY COST-ALLOCATION METHOD?

15   A.       Staff witness Douglas B. Jester describes an hourly cost method that it states is

16            conceptually similar to the National Association of Regulatory Utility

17            Commissioners’ Probability-of-Dispatch (“POD”) method. 1 Staff recommends that

18            the approach be examined after this proceeding and that the Company present a new

19            cost-allocation approach in a future rate case. 2



     1
         See Prepared Direct Testimony of Douglas B. Jester (“Jester Direct”) at p. 29:11–20.
     2
         Id. at p. 30:5–8.




                                                   3
                                      NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                           Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                              Walmart Inc.


 1   Q.       DOES STAFF RECOMMEND IMPLEMENTING THAT NEW METHOD TO

2             RESET CLASS REVENUE RESPONSIBILITY IN THIS CASE?

3    A.       No. Staff does not recommend a specific change to cost-of-service allocations in this

4             case. Staff states that the case schedule does not permit a complete reworking of the

5             cost-of-service study (“COSS”) and instead recommends banding and phasing in the

 6            present case. 3

 7   Q.       WHAT IS WALMART’S POSITION ON A SUPPLEMENTAL OR

 8            ALTERNATIVE CLASS COST-OF-SERVICE PRESENTATION?

 9   A.       Walmart does not oppose a properly filed, transparent supplemental presentation,

10            alongside the Company’s existing methodology. An alternative presentation can be

11            useful if it identifies the underlying data, assumptions, functionalization,

12            classification, allocators, and resulting class impacts so that the parties and the

13            Commission can determine the best reflection of cost causation. Walmart does not

14            oppose consideration of the proposed hourly method in the future process Staff

15            recommends, 4 but at this time does not support adoption of the methodology.




     3
         Id. at 28:18–29:10.
     4
         Id. at 30:4–8; 64:17–65:10.




                                                4
                                 NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                      Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                         Walmart Inc.


 1   Q.   WHAT SHOULD THE COMMISSION REQUIRE BEFORE USING AN

 2        ALTERNATIVE          PRESENTATION           TO     RESET      CLASS       REVENUE

 3        RESPONSIBILITY?

 4   A.   The Commission should require an evidentiary record sufficient to test the

 5        methodology and its consequences. A different result driven by a different cost

 6        allocation approach, by itself, does not establish that the alternative methodology

 7        more accurately reflects cost causation. The affected classes should have the

 8        opportunity to examine the inputs, assumptions, and rate-design effects before an

 9        alternative study is used to change class revenue responsibility.

10   Q.   WHAT IS WALMART’S POSITION ON REVENUE ALLOCATION?

11   A.   Revenue allocation should be informed by an accurate class cost-of-service study.

12        Once the Commission has determined the final revenue requirement and the costs

13        properly attributed to each class, it may use those results to move classes toward cost

14        of service, subject to the Commission’s judgment concerning gradualism and

15        customer impacts. Walmart continues not to object to the Company’s proposed

16        revenue allocation at the appropriate final revenue requirement. If the Commission

17        directs further work on production-allocation methodology, that work should be

18        completed with transparent data, adequate modeling detail, and an opportunity for

19        all affected classes to participate before the results are used to reset class revenue

20        responsibility.




                                             5
                                    NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                         Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                            Walmart Inc.


 1   Q.     WHAT         IS     WALMART’S             UNDERSTANDING                OF   CCAE’S

 2          RECOMMENDATION REGARDING POD?

 3   A.     CCAE witness Ron Nelson recommends that the Commission require the Company

4           to apply a Probability-of-Dispatch (“POD”) method to allocate demand-related

5           production costs among customer classes and to prepare new revenue-allocation and

 6          rate-design proposals based on the resulting class cost-of-service study. 5 CCAE’s

 7          POD study would reduce the Residential class cost of service by approximately $8.3

 8          million and increase the Large Power class cost of service by approximately $3.9

 9          million. 6

10   Q.     DOES WALMART SUPPORT ADOPTING CCAE’S POD RESULTS TO

11          RESET CLASS REVENUE RESPONSIBILITY IN THIS CASE?

12   A.     No. CCAE’s proposed POD results represent a material class-wide reallocation of

13          generation costs. 7 Walmart does not oppose transparent consideration of an

14          alternative cost-of-service presentation. Before the Commission uses the POD

15          results to change class revenue responsibility, parties should have a full opportunity

16          to evaluate the underlying hourly data, modeling assumptions, cost-causation

17          rationale, allocation results, and resulting rate-design effects.




     5
       See Direct Testimony of Ron Nelson (“Nelson Direct”) at pp. 97:19 – 98:2.
     6
       See id. at p. 93:4–12 and p. 94 at Table RN-2.
     7
       See id. at 92:3–8 (Table RN-1).




                                                6
                                      NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                           Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                              Walmart Inc.


1    Q.       WHY IS THAT CAUTION IMPORTANT TO WALMART?

2    A.       A class cost-of-service study is a tool for assigning shared costs using measures that

3             reasonably reflect cost causation. A change in methodology can produce a different

4             result, but the existence of a different result does not itself establish that the new

5             result is more accurate. CCAE’s proposed POD result would increase the cost

6             responsibility of the Large Power class by more than 40 percent in CCAE’s

 7            presentation. 8 Before that result is used to set rates, the Commission should have an

 8            evidentiary record sufficient to test the inputs, assumptions, and consequences of the

 9            proposed methodology.

10   Q.       IS WALMART ASKING THE COMMISSION TO RESOLVE THE

11            BROADER METHODOLOGICAL DEBATE IN THIS CASE?

12   A.       No. Staff identifies concerns with the existing production allocators but does not

13            recommend a complete reworking of the cost-of-service study in this case because

14            of the time required to develop new load statistics and carry them through a final

15            allocation. Staff instead recommends that the Company propose a modified

16            approach in its next rate case. 9 That approach is a more balanced and measured path

17            than adopting an untested class-wide reallocation now.




     8
         See id. at pp. 92:1 – 93:10 (Table RN-2).
     9
         See Jester Direct at p. 17:20–18:8, pp. 28:18–29:10, and p. 48:1–7.




                                                    7
                                       NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                            Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                               Walmart Inc.


 1   Q.        WHAT IS WALMART’S POSITION ON REVENUE ALLOCATION IN

 2             LIGHT OF THOSE POSITIONS?

 3   A.        Walmart continues to not oppose the Company’s proposed revenue allocation at the

 4             appropriate final authorized revenue requirement. The Commission should not use

 5             CCAE’s alternative allocation to increase Large Power rates in this case. If the

 6             Commission directs further work on production allocation methodology, that work

 7             should be completed, in a future general rate case showing, with transparent data,

 8             adequate modeling detail, and an opportunity for all affected classes to participate

 9             before the results are used to reset class revenue responsibility.

10

11   Battery Capacity Costs, Cost of Service, and Revenue Allocation
12   Q.    WHAT IS WALMART’S UNDERSTANDING OF THE NMDOJ’S POSITION

13             AS TO THE APPROPRIATE RECOVERY METHOD FOR RENEWABLE

14             PORTFOLIO STANDARD (“RPS”) BATTERY CAPACITY COSTS?

15   A.        The NMDOJ recommends that the Commission retain the Santa Teresa and Carne

16             battery-capacity costs in the RPS Cost Rider rather than move them to base rates. 10

17             DOJ recommends leaving Buena Vista 1 in base rates because the prior

18             Recommended Decision directed the Company to seek recovery of those costs in its

19             next base-rate case. 11 DOJ further recommends that, if the Commission places any




     10
          See Direct Testimony of Jamal Mamkhezri (“Mamkhezri Direct”) at p. 46:1042–49.
     11
          Id. at p. 46:1050–52.




                                                     8
                                        NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                             Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                                Walmart Inc.


1              battery-capacity costs in base rates, it require annual reconciliation of actual charges

2              against amounts recovered in rates and require the Company to demonstrate the

 3             residential-class effect in its cost-of-service workpapers. 12

 4

 5   Q.        WHAT IS WALMART’S CONCERN REGARDING WHETHER THE

 6             COMPANY’S BATTERY CAPACITY COSTS SHOULD REMAIN IN THE

 7             RPS”) COST RIDER OR MOVE TO BASE RATES?

 8   A.        Walmart’s principal concern is that the Company demonstrate the proper cost-

 9             recovery mechanism and allocation basis for each cost. The Company should

10             identify the nature of the battery-capacity costs, the applicable Commission

11             direction, the proposed allocation method, and the resulting class impacts. A

12             recovery mechanism should not be selected in a manner that shifts costs among

13             customer classes without transparent support.

14   Q.        SHOULD THE COMMISSION PRESERVE CUSTOMER PROTECTIONS

15             IF ANY BATTERY CAPACITY COSTS MOVE TO BASE RATES?

16   A.        Yes. If the Commission permits a migration of battery-capacity costs from the RPS

17             Cost Rider to base rates, the Company should maintain a transparent reconciliation

18             or other auditable mechanism sufficient to prevent over-recovery and should provide

19             a clear class-impact analysis before the change takes effect. Those protections are




     12
          Id. at pp. 46:1055 – 47;1061.




                                                   9
                                      NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                           Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                              Walmart Inc.


 1            consistent with Walmart’s recommendation that rates reflect demonstrable cost

 2            causation and avoid double recovery or interclass cost shifts.

 3   Q.       DOES WALMART SUPPORT MOVING THE COMPANY’S BATTERY

 4            CAPACITY COSTS INTO BASE RATES?

 5   A.       Yes. Walmart supports base-rate treatment of battery capacity costs that are properly

 6            included in the Company’s revenue requirement. That treatment permits those costs

 7            to be reflected in the class cost-of-service study, where their functionalization,

 8            classification, and assignment can be examined by the parties and the Commission

 9            before revenue allocation is set. The Company identifies the payments at issue as

10            battery capacity charges and explains that battery storage provides firm capacity and

11            operational flexibility. 13

12   Q.       WHY IS THAT REVIEW IMPORTANT?

13   A.       A cost-of-service study must first identify the utility function served by a cost,

14            classify the cost according to the service it provides, and then assign or allocate the

15            cost using measures that reasonably reflect cost causation. Battery resources can

16            provide capacity, reliability, energy-shifting, and renewable-integration services.

17            Their treatment in the study should follow the evidence concerning the particular

18            resource, contract, and dispatch, rather than the label of a rider or a predetermined

19            allocation result. 14



     13
          See Direct Testimony of Victor Martinez at p. 13:2–17, p. 16:8–17, and p. 17:6–13.
     14
          Id. at p. 13:2–17; see also Direct Testimony of Adrian Hernandez at p. 7:1–8.




                                                  10
                                      NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                           Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                              Walmart Inc.


 1   Q.       HOW DOES THAT RELATE TO REVENUE ALLOCATION?

 2   A.       The COSS study establishes the best available measure of each class’s cost

 3            responsibility, informing the appropriate revenue allocation. Revenue allocation

 4            determines how the final authorized revenue requirement will be collected from the

 5            classes. If battery capacity costs remain outside base rates, the study used for base-

 6            rate allocation does not reflect the full cost of the system that customers use. Putting

 7            the costs in base rates therefore provides the accurate, transparent starting point

 8            needed before the Commission decides whether and how quickly to move classes

 9            toward cost of service.

10   Q.       DOES THAT POSITION REQUIRE THE COMMISSION TO ACCEPT A

11            PARTICULAR DEMAND OR ENERGY CLASSIFICATION FOR ALL

12            BATTERY COSTS?

13   A.       No. Walmart does not prejudge the appropriate classification of each battery cost.

14            The relevant point is that the Company should identify and include the recoverable

15            costs in the study, identify the service provided, and support the resulting allocation

16            with transparent evidence. The Commission can then evaluate the class impacts on

17            a complete record. An estimate of the difference produced by two allocation methods

18            is useful information, but it is not a reason to exclude the cost from the cost-of-

19            service study. 15




     15
          See Mamkhezri Direct at p. 43:980–986; p. 44:987–999; and p. 46:1041–1060.




                                                 11
                                 NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                      Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                         Walmart Inc.


1    Q.   HOW SHOULD THE COMMISSION DISTINGUISH COMMON SYSTEM

2         BATTERY COSTS FROM COSTS CAUSED BY A QUALIFYING NEW

 3        LARGE-LOAD CUSTOMER?

 4   A.   Existing, shared system resources should be examined and allocated through the

 5        cost-of-service study. Direct assignment should apply only when the Company

 6        demonstrates that a particular incremental resource commitment, facility, or other

 7        cost was caused by a qualifying new large-load customer and identifies the related

 8        annual revenue requirement. In that circumstance, the customer should bear the

 9        actual incremental cost and risk through appropriate tariff and Energy Service

10        Agreement (“ESA”) provisions, and only the residual common-system cost should

11        be allocated through the study.

12   Q.   WHY IS THAT DIRECT-ASSIGNMENT SAFEGUARD IMPORTANT FOR

13        NEW VERY LARGE LOAD?

14   A.   A new resource commitment may carry current contractual, capital, and financing

15        costs that differ from the embedded costs of the existing system. If an incremental

16        resource is caused by a qualifying new customer but is instead spread through an

17        average embedded allocation, the customer may pay less than the cost it caused

18        while established customers bear a portion of the new, higher-cost commitment.

19        Direct assignment of demonstrated incremental costs avoids that result. It also

20        protects the qualifying customer by requiring identification of the actual




                                            12
                                      NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                           Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                              Walmart Inc.


 1            commitment and by preventing recovery of the same cost through both a customer-

2             specific charge and general rates.

3

 4   Large Load Tariffs and Customer-Specific Cost Protection
 5   Q.   DOES WALMART AGREE THAT NEW, EXTRAORDINARY LOAD MAY

6             REQUIRE          CUSTOMER-SPECIFIC            PROTECTION AGAINST               COST

 7            SHIFTS?

 8   A.       Yes. The record identifies legitimate concerns when a proposed new load requires

 9            customer-dedicated facilities, accelerated investment, or a resource commitment that

10            would not otherwise be needed. In those circumstances, the customer should bear

11            the identifiable incremental costs and financial exposure caused by its service, using

12            appropriate ESA, billing-demand, facility-charge, collateral, and termination

13            provisions. 16

14   Q.       DOES THAT PRINCIPLE SUPPORT AUTOMATICALLY ASSIGNING ALL

15            COSTS OF NEW GENERATION OR ALL LARGE-CUSTOMER LOAD TO

16            A SPECIAL RATE?

17   A.       Not necessarily. Cost protection must remain tied to demonstrated cost causation.

18            CLC/DAC recommends that all generation resources added for Rate Nos. 50 and 51

19            customers be collected directly from those customers. That proposal may identify

20            issues for future Commission consideration, but it does not establish that every


     16
          See Nelson Direct at pp. 9:11–10:3 and pp. 54:12–57:18.




                                                   13
                                      NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                           Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                              Walmart Inc.


1             generation investment occurring while a large customer takes service is caused by

2             that customer. The Company should identify the particular incremental resource

3             commitment, facilities, timing, and annual revenue requirement attributable to the

4             qualifying customer, and should credit costs already recovered through customer

5             contributions, facility charges, or other mechanisms. 17

 6   Q.       HOW       DOES       WALMART’S          APPROACH             PROTECT       EXISTING

 7            CUSTOMERS?

 8   A.       Walmart’s approach protects existing customers by requiring the qualifying

 9            customer to bear the costs it causes and by preventing double recovery. The ESA

10            and associated tariff terms should identify the committed capacity, load-ramp

11            schedule, dedicated facilities, incremental resource commitments, security, and

12            recovery mechanisms.

13   Q.       SHOULD THE            COMMISSION APPLY RATE                    NOS.     50 AND        51

14            AUTOMATICALLY TO EXISTING CUSTOMERS OR ORDINARY

15            COMMERCIAL GROWTH?

16   A.       No. DOD/FEA likewise recommends an express grandfathering provision for

17            existing customers and existing load. Walmart agrees with the basic principle that a

18            new large-load framework should be prospective and should not automatically alter

19            the default rate classification of an existing retail, commercial, industrial, logistics,




     17
          See Direct Testimony of Andrew K. Harriger at pp. 23:9 –25:18.




                                                 14
                                      NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                           Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                              Walmart Inc.


 1            warehouse, manufacturing, or charging customer merely because of load growth,

 2            technology, or a numerical threshold. 18

 3   Q.       WHAT SHOULD THE COMMISSION REQUIRE TO DETERMINE

 4            WHETHER A CUSTOMER BELONGS IN A SPECIAL LARGE-LOAD

 5            CLASS?

 6   A.       The Commission should require a like-with-like, objective showing. The relevant

 7            characteristics are the magnitude and timing of new incremental load at a single

 8            point of delivery, load shape, load factor, dedicated or incremental infrastructure,

 9            resource commitment, and stranded-cost risk. Customer end use or corporate

10            identity is not a cost driver. Nor should separate sites, meters, facilities, affiliates,

11            retail locations, distribution operations, or electric-vehicle charging facilities be

12            aggregated to meet a threshold.

13   Q.       DOES WALMART CONTINUE TO SUPPORT ITS 75-MEGAWATT

14            SINGLE-POINT-OF-DELIVERY APPLICABILITY RECOMMENDATION?

15   A.       Yes. The 75-megawatt threshold is an administrable screen for the exceptional new

16            loads that may create distinct infrastructure and commitment risks. It should not

17            replace the necessary cost-causation showing, but it avoids subjecting ordinary large

18            customers with existing, predictable load profiles to a specialized tariff merely

19            because they exceed the Company’s proposed 10- or 30-megawatt thresholds.




     18
          See Direct Testimony of Larry Blank at pp. 44:5–45:9.




                                                  15
                                       NMPRC Case No. 25-00082-UT
                            Rebuttal Testimony of Dr. Jaime Lyndsey McGovern
                                               Walmart Inc.


 1             DOD/FEA similarly recognizes that the record does not establish support for Rate

2              No. 51 as a separate rate class beginning at 10 megawatts without a load-factor

 3             requirement. 19

 4   Q.        HOW SHOULD THE COMMISSION ADDRESS CONCERNS ABOUT THE

 5             COMPANY’S PROPOSED LARGE-LOAD RATE LEVELS?

 6   A.        The Commission should require updated cost-of-service and rate-design support that

 7             reflects the final eligibility criteria and the actual cost characteristics of qualifying

 8             customers. A uniform requirement that every specialized-tariff customer pay no less

 9             than the effective rate under another schedule would not itself be cost based;

10             different voltage, load factor, load shape, facilities, and contractual protections can

11             produce different costs. The appropriate safeguard is a transparent demonstration

12             that the qualifying customer pays the identifiable costs and risks caused by its

13             service, without shifting those costs to other customers and without collecting them

14             twice. 20

15   Q.        DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY.

16   A.        Yes.
